memory_update.text: LOPE is the cleanest public services-provider exposure to accredited online degree enablement because it reports university partner service revenue, partner enrollments, and revenue-share contract changes.
COUR should remain in the universe despite a sub-$1B market cap because it is a direct modular university-degree platform candidate and may fit the shift away from legacy full-service OPM economics.

STRA, ATGE, and PRDO are better classified as accredited online degree asset owners/direct customers rather than OPM suppliers; they provide direct exposure to online degree demand but carry federal aid, accreditation, and outcomes risks.

2U should be tracked as formerly public and now private after Chapter 11; its restructuring is a negative model signal for high-debt, high-revenue-share OPM economics, not proof that all online degree demand is weak.

Need a separate pass for private OPMs, university LMS vendors, CRM/student-success software suppliers, and nonprofit university customers because this Layer 1B pass was constrained to direct public companies and obvious leaders.
LOPE is the cleanest US-listed direct university-services / OPM-adjacent public candidate for accredited online-degree enablement.
COUR is below the preferred USD 1B market-cap filter in the latest finance snapshot but remains an exception because it is a public modular online-degree and workforce-learning platform.
GHC provides indirect exposure through Kaplan; treat as education-services exposure inside a diversified holding company rather than a pure OPM comp.
STRA and ATGE are better classified as accredited online/workforce education operators and regulated-capacity proxies, not scarce third-party OPM suppliers.

The listed-universe chokepoint appears to be shifting away from pure legacy revenue-share OPMs toward modular platforms, internal university-services capacity, employer-funded pathways, and regulated healthcare workforce programs.

Several important node assets are not currently US-listed or are private/taken-private, including 2U, Risepoint/Academic Partnerships, Instructure/Canvas, Anthology/Blackboard, Boundless Learning, and Noodle; this limits public-market purity.

Need a follow-up pass on LMS, identity/credentialing, proctoring, student information systems, clinical placement systems, and Title IV compliance vendors; many may be private or embedded inside larger software companies.
Add COUR as the clearest US-listed direct online-degree platform candidate after 2U's restructuring/private status; verify degree-segment materiality before ranking.
Add LOPE as an underappreciated OPM-like services-agreement company with direct tuition-share exposure, technology services, academic services, marketing, counseling, and back-office support.
Add STRA as an adjacent adult-learning and employer-channel beneficiary; its ETS segment may map to lower-cost modular workforce education rather than legacy OPM economics.

For this node, second-order chokepoints include student information systems, financial-aid/compliance workflows, CRM/advising, LMS-integrated video, and student-success analytics, not just outsourced marketing.

Several major OPM assets are private or no longer pure-play public exposures: 2U/edX is private post-restructuring, Risepoint/Academic Partnerships is private, Boundless Learning is private after Pearson's OPM sale, and Instructure/Canvas is private after KKR acquisition.

Potential additional public second-order names for later passes include Salesforce for Education Cloud, Microsoft/LinkedIn Learning, Zoom for virtual delivery, and public consulting integrators, but their exposure to the OPM node is likely small relative to total revenue and needs stronger evidence.
